impact.title: What it adds up to
impact.narrative: In 9 months of production work he merged 412 pull requests adding 410K+ lines, across three AI products and the infrastructure under them: a voice assistant with long-term memory, a computer-vision inventory product for insurance claims, and a multi-tenant platform that runs a private team of AI agents for every workspace. The pattern repeats across all of it — measure before claiming (held-out evals, concurrency benchmarks), migrate in stages instead of big-bang cutovers, and treat idempotency and concurrency as product features. 197 commits are co-authored with AI coding agents: he builds AI, with AI.

points.claim: Re-architected per-item pricing as a parallel retail-search fan-out with LLM ranking, projected in the PR at ~5s versus ~60s before.
Validated a vision fix on a held-out, human-labelled set: exact-count rate 81% → 83%, over-count 0.53 → 0.43 per photo-run.

Auth moved in stages, never a big-bang cutover: SimpleJWT to Firebase on one product, a phased move to Better Auth that kept row-level security on another, and a new registration control plane for a third.
Re-platformed a production AI product onto AWS EKS with Terraform, SQS workers and idempotent at-least-once processing.
Got a fix merged upstream into an open-source agent runtime.

chapters.title: Prologue: Carbon on the Chain
chapters.kicker: Research roots: a building's carbon footprint, made tamper-proof.
chapters.narrative: It starts in construction research: material quantities pulled out of Revit BIM models, embodied carbon computed, results written to Ethereum so no one could quietly edit them. When on-chain costs bit, the prototype moved to PostgreSQL — ship the version that works.

impact.claim: Carbon records nobody can quietly edit: Revit BIM material data extracted via pyRevit, embodied carbon computed and written to an Ethereum ledger.
Procurement that survives real costs: a BIM-driven Solidity prototype re-based onto PostgreSQL.

chapters.title: Nights, Notebooks, Prototypes
chapters.kicker: After a silent summer, the commit graph lights up with self-directed AI builds.
chapters.narrative: Nobody assigned any of this. A Graph-RAG chatbot over a raw email archive, run on GPU in a notebook; an LLM parser that turns emailed purchase orders into structured records with duplicate detection; an IoT sensor rig with anomaly detection and a live dashboard; real-time speech experiments; and a public portfolio rebuilt commit by commit. It was practice — and it is exactly the toolkit the next chapter needed.

impact.claim: Questions answered over a raw email archive: hybrid retrieval plus a GPU-accelerated Graph-RAG notebook.
Purchase-order emails turned into structured, de-duplicated records automatically, with Gemini doing the parsing.
Sensor anomalies flagged live: an IoT rig with ML anomaly detection streaming to a dashboard.

chapters.title: A Voice That Remembers
chapters.kicker: First production role: a voice-first AI assistant with long-term memory.
chapters.narrative: Joining an AI venture studio, the first hard product was a voice assistant that remembers. He moved its real-time loop from GPT-4o Realtime to Gemini Live, gave it pgvector recall over past sessions, embedded photos together with their AI analysis for multimodal memory, and built an LLM-maintained wiki that compiles conversations into interlinked pages. Then the unglamorous half that makes it real: on-device iOS speech, a microphone that sometimes stayed silent on cold start, and intermittent production not-found errors traced back through server logs.

impact.claim: Snappier voice replies: audio flush threshold cut from ~1.5s to ~0.3s by moving real-time voice from GPT-4o Realtime to Gemini Live.
An assistant that remembers what it heard and saw: pgvector recall over past sessions plus joint image + text embeddings.
Conversations become a living knowledge base: sessions compiled into interlinked wiki pages by an async two-model pipeline, searched with hybrid wiki + vector retrieval.
No more silent first sessions on iPhone: native on-device speech-to-text and a cold-start microphone fix that probes for real audio and retries.
Existing accounts carried across an auth migration (SimpleJWT to Firebase) with a verified path, and intermittent production 404s root-caused from server logs.

chapters.title: Eyes on Every Object
chapters.kicker: The flagship: a computer-vision home-inventory product for insurance claims.
chapters.narrative: Photograph a room; get back an itemised, priced inventory ready for an insurance claim. He built the two-pass vision pipeline at its core — detect every object, then identify each from a full-resolution crop — and judged fixes against human-labelled photos instead of eyeballing them. Pricing became a parallel retail-search fan-out with LLM ranking and a deterministic median, the AI pipeline moved onto per-upload task workers, and auth moved in phases to a new provider without breaking row-level security. The biggest codebase of the run, end to end: web, mobile, database and model calls.

impact.claim: Full inventories from a single photo: on a real claims photo, items found went from 1 to 11 with a detect-then-identify vision pipeline that reads each object from a full-resolution crop.
Counts you can trust, proven on held-out data: exact-count rate 81% → 83% and over-count 0.53 → 0.43 per photo-run, under a pre-registered evaluation of 33 photos and 146 human-labelled counts.
Prices in seconds, not a minute: projected in the PR at ~5s per item, down from ~60s, via a parallel retail-search fan-out with LLM ranking and a deterministic median.
Uploads processed in parallel: projected in the PR to take a 6-photo job from ~9 min to ~3 min with per-upload task workers and retries.
No more dying workers or double-processed photos under load: out-of-memory kills at queue concurrency 10 fixed, and duplicate photos now decided atomically under a lock.
Users moved to a new auth provider with no big-bang cutover: Better Auth on web, then mobile with Apple sign-in, row-level security preserved via short-lived compatible JWTs.
A claim-ready product end to end: phone-first capture wizard, professional review console and a claim-support PDF dossier, shipped in one 45-PR production release.

chapters.title: Rebuilt for the Cloud
chapters.kicker: 321 commits in 16 days: the product re-platformed AWS-native.
chapters.narrative: Then the same product, rebuilt from the ground up on AWS. Heavy LLM work moved onto an SQS worker pipeline that streams per-stage progress to clients over SSE; Terraform modules stood up web, API and workers on a shared EKS cluster with per-stage Postgres; schema migrations ran as a checksum-ledgered Kubernetes Job before every rollout. An architecture review closed with workers that stay correct under at-least-once delivery.

impact.claim: Long LLM jobs no longer block requests: heavy work moved onto an async SQS worker pipeline that streams per-stage progress to clients over SSE.
Repeatable infrastructure: web, API and workers deployed by Terraform onto a shared EKS platform with ingress routing and per-stage Postgres.
Schema changes that can't half-apply: a checksum-ledger migration runner executed as a one-shot Kubernetes Job before every rollout.
Correct under at-least-once delivery: idempotent worker callbacks and a closed worker-to-database back door, across ~25k lines of architecture fixes.
Deploys guarded by tests: an audit-driven suite catching env drift, worker boot failures and broken readiness probes.

chapters.title: Agents That Listen
chapters.kicker: Turning meetings into agent memory — without leaking a word.
chapters.narrative: Next problem: feed an organisation's meetings to its AI agents without building a surveillance machine. He built a transcript ingest that denies every meeting by default, a router where each person connects their own account over OAuth and nothing is stored, and a derived knowledge graph — people extracted deterministically, projects and concepts by an LLM with evidence quotes, cached by content hash. When the first users got stuck hand-wiring webhooks, he shipped a one-click chat install and a rules-first routing engine with a durable outbox.

impact.claim: No meeting reaches an agent unless approved: a deny-by-default allowlist in front of transcript ingestion.
Each person controls their own meeting data: per-user OAuth, nothing stored, tenants isolated by row-level security.
Meetings become a queryable knowledge graph: people extracted deterministically, projects and concepts by an LLM with evidence quotes, cached by content hash.
Routing users can actually set up: a rules-first engine with signed webhooks and a durable outbox, backed by 176 tests against the real tenant boundary.
Setup that used to stall first users became one click: an OAuth Slack install replacing hand-copied webhook URLs.

chapters.title: An Operating System for Agents
chapters.kicker: A multi-tenant platform where every workspace gets its own team of AI agents.
chapters.narrative: The latest arc: a multi-tenant platform that provisions a private team of AI agents for each workspace on Kubernetes. He wrote its registration control plane, per-tenant agent rosters, per-agent skill allowlists, owner-approved tasks that agents propose from meetings, and an audited superadmin panel. The hard parts were distributed-systems parts — stale queue messages fenced off with instance and operation IDs, terminal failures that stopped retrying forever, agents hot-added without restarting the gateway. Along the way a fix landed upstream in the open-source agent runtime itself, and on the side he steered an open LLM by pushing two neurons and came full circle with an AI agent for Revit.

impact.claim: Any company can sign up and get its own agent team: a registration control plane with OAuth, verified email, rate limits and onboarding (~27k lines, 104 files).
Each tenant chooses its agents and what they may do: per-tenant rosters replacing a fixed list baked into the Helm chart, plus per-agent skill allowlists.

Stale queue messages can no longer touch a replacement workspace: provisioning fenced with instance and operation IDs, terminal failures no longer retried forever — backed by 394 tests, 110 of them lifecycle cases.
No outage to add an agent, no hung new tenants: agents hot-added without a gateway restart, and a boot hang that left new tenants waiting ~40 min fixed.
Meetings turn into work, with a human in the loop: transcripts routed to the agent each person picks, with idempotent retries, and agent-proposed tasks that the owner approves.
Secrets stay secret: every value masked until revealed, every reveal and admin action audited.
A fix merged upstream into an open-source agent runtime: managed coding-CLI runtime bump and regenerated protocol schemas.
